clue.text: The scornful lady's gentlewoman

parts.note: points to the waiting-woman in Beaumont and Fletcher's play The Scornful Lady, whose name became a byword for any lady's maid

explanation.surface: A question about the attendant of a disdainful mistress.
explanation.walkthrough: In Beaumont and Fletcher's comedy The Scornful Lady the waiting-gentlewoman bears this name, and from her it passed into English as a general word for a lady's maid.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the play's waiting-gentlewoman later became a common noun for a lady's maid.

clue.text: Gap author possibly found in signed copy

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of gap and author could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A writer's gap turns up in a book the writer has signed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges GAP AUTHOR into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A book bearing the writer's own signature is called by this name, as in an inscribed edition.

clue.text: Sarah, gift of Isis and a fantastic read

definitions.text: Sarah, gift of Isis and a fantastic read

parts.words: Sarah, gift of Isis and a fantastic read
parts.note: the surname of the fantasy novelist Sarah ..., whose name in Greek means given by the goddess Isis, and whose books are fantasy reading

explanation.surface: A woman called Sarah, a present from the goddess, and a novel full of wonders.
explanation.walkthrough: Three hints to one name: the American fantasy writer Sarah Isidore (the Daughters of Bast trilogy), the Greek name's meaning 'gift of Isis', and 'a fantastic read' for her fantasy fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek personal name means 'gift of Isis', and it is also the surname of the fantasy author Sarah Isidore.

clue.text: Poetic measure of those opposed to former times

parts.note: people who are against something are antis
the past is former times

explanation.surface: A verse foot belonging to people who reject the old days.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a classical metrical foot of four syllables, an iamb followed by a trochee.

clue.text: Reported bloomer affected writer

indicators.note: reported means we take the sound of the word, as if it were spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: a lily is a flower, something that blooms

explanation.surface: A flower, it is said, influenced an author.
explanation.walkthrough: John Lyly wrote Euphues, whose ornate style gave us 'euphuism', so he is the affected writer; 'bloomer' is a flower, not a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan John Lyly is known for a mannered, ornate prose style.

clue.text: Bad actor in single combat awarded Prix Goncourt

indicators.note: in places the bad actor inside the word for single combat

parts.note: a duel is a fight between two people
a ham is an overacting performer

explanation.surface: A poor actor in a fight scene somehow takes a top literary prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Georges Duhamel won the Prix Goncourt in 1918 for Civilisation; the definition describes him rather than naming him.
explanation.definitionFit: The French writer Georges Duhamel received France's premier literary prize in 1918.

clue.text: Did he bracket World War I, this author to keep up with?

definitions.text: Did he bracket World War I, this author to keep up with?

parts.words: Did he bracket World War I, this author to keep up with?
parts.note: In Parenthesis is a long poem about the First World War, so its writer put the war in brackets; 'keep up with the' family name is the idiom

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone put the Great War in parentheses, and whom we must keep pace with.
explanation.walkthrough: David Jones wrote In Parenthesis about his service in the First World War, so he 'bracketed' it; 'keeping up with the Joneses' supplies the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh poet-painter David Jones wrote In Parenthesis, a war epic, and shares a surname with the proverbial neighbours.

clue.text: In another sense, 13 may make haste

indicators.note: may make says the letters of haste can be formed into a different word

explanation.surface: The cross-reference may hurry things along.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is ANATHEMATA, defined there as votive offerings; in its other sense an anathema is a thing cursed or loathed. 'may make' rearranges HASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Anathemas, in the sense of things detested, are things one loathes.

clue.text: A tragic adaptation of D' Avenant

definitions.text: A tragic adaptation of D' Avenant

parts.words: A tragic adaptation of D' Avenant
parts.note: Sir William Davenant produced an altered version of a Shakespeare tragedy for the Restoration stage

explanation.surface: A sad reworking by a seventeenth-century dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Davenant's Restoration version of Shakespeare's Scottish play, with added songs and witches, held the stage for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: Davenant rewrote Shakespeare's Scottish tragedy in 1664, and his version was long performed.

clue.text: Platonic dialogue with a tart upset Aristophanes comedy

indicators.note: the answer with the other pieces added makes the comedy, so those pieces are taken away from it

parts.note: Lysistrata is Aristophanes' play about a sex strike

indicators.note: upset means the word tart is turned upside down, read backwards in a down light

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A philosophical dialogue plus a toppled pastry makes a Greek comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer with A and TART upset (TRAT) makes Aristophanes' LYSISTRATA, so take TRAT and A from the play's name. Plato's Lysis is on friendship.
explanation.definitionFit: Lysis is Plato's short dialogue about friendship.

clue.text: Dickens hero wants another card?

definitions.meaning: Oliver of the workhouse novel bears this surname
in pontoon a player calls this word to be dealt another card

explanation.surface: Does Oliver ask the dealer for one more?
explanation.walkthrough: In pontoon (the British card game like blackjack), a player who wants another card face up says 'twist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver's surname, and the call for an extra card in pontoon.

clue.text: Italian writer is cut, unfortunately, from old law book

parts.note: Primo Levi was an Italian author

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests the words is cut have gone wrong and are jumbled

explanation.surface: An Italian author suffers a sad cut from an ancient legal text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges IS CUT into TICUS, which follows LEVI.
explanation.definitionFit: The third book of the Bible sets out the priestly laws of the ancient Israelites.

clue.text: Describes work with many explanatory notes?

definitions.text: Describes work with many explanatory notes?

parts.words: Describes work with many explanatory notes?
parts.note: a gloss is an explanatory note, so a text full of them is jokingly described by the adjective that usually means shiny

explanation.surface: A term for a heavily annotated text.
explanation.walkthrough: A gloss is a marginal explanation; the adjective usually means shiny, as in a magazine, but here means full of glosses.
explanation.definitionFit: Glosses are explanatory notes, so a text packed with them is full of glosses.

clue.text: It's all Greek for Joyce protagonist

definitions.text: It's all Greek for Joyce protagonist

parts.words: It's all Greek for Joyce protagonist
parts.note: Joyce's Ulysses takes its title from the Latin name of the Homeric hero; the Greek name is wanted

explanation.surface: Joyce's hero is incomprehensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's all Greek' looks like 'baffling', but means the Greek form: Ulysses is the Latin name of the hero Homer named differently.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's wandering king of Ithaca is called Ulysses in Latin, the name of Joyce's novel.

clue.text: Some votive offerings of 5

parts.note: the long poem by the writer at 5 down takes its title from a Greek word for things dedicated to a god

explanation.surface: Gifts left at a shrine by another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 5 is DAVID JONES, whose 1952 poem The Anathemata is named for things set apart as offerings.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek plural names things dedicated to a god, and it is the title of David Jones's 1952 poem.

clue.text: De Sade laughingly includes Forster heroine

indicators.note: includes says the answer is held within the run of letters of de sade laughingly

explanation.surface: The Marquis's work, amusingly, features a character from A Passage to India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' points to the run deSADE LAughingly; Adela Quested is the young Englishwoman in A Passage to India.
explanation.definitionFit: Adela Quested is the central young woman of Forster's A Passage to India.

clue.text: Like the Houses of Parliament, or new black letter?

parts.note: neo- is a prefix meaning new
black letter is the Gothic style of typeface

explanation.surface: Is Westminster's style a fresh kind of heavy script?
explanation.walkthrough: The Palace of Westminster was rebuilt in the 1840s in the Gothic Revival style; black letter is the heavy medieval script also called Gothic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Palace of Westminster is the best-known building of the Victorian Gothic Revival.

clue.text: Mackenzie's idea of where we live

definitions.text: Mackenzie's idea of where we live

parts.words: Mackenzie's idea of where we live
parts.note: Compton Mackenzie wrote a 1931 novel whose title describes the road we live on

explanation.surface: A novelist's notion of our home address.
explanation.walkthrough: Compton Mackenzie's novel Our Street (1931) sketches the people of one London road; the title is literally where we live.
explanation.definitionFit: Compton Mackenzie's novel title names the road belonging to us.

clue.text: Stephen King book, richest in rewrite

indicators.note: a rewrite rearranges the words richest in into a new order

explanation.surface: A horror novel revised by the wealthiest author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewrite' rearranges RICHEST IN; King's novel is about a murderous car of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen King's 1983 novel is named after its possessed Plymouth Fury.

clue.text: Name of section (like Bleak or Lear?)

definitions.meaning: a page in a book bearing only the short title, before the title page or a part
Bleak is part of Bleak House and Lear part of King Lear, each a portion of a title

explanation.surface: What do you call a part of a book like the start of a Dickens title?
explanation.walkthrough: In printing, this is the page with the bare title before the main title page or a section; Bleak and Lear are each only half of a title.
explanation.definitionFit: The bibliographic term names a page with a short title, and literally a portion of a full name.

clue.text: Bloom, perhaps, formerly on Belgian throne

definitions.meaning: Joyce's Mr Bloom in Ulysses has this first name
three kings of the Belgians have borne this name

explanation.surface: A flower once ruled Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloom' looks like a flower but is Joyce's Leopold Bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: The first name of Joyce's Mr Bloom, and the name of three Belgian kings.

clue.text: Versifier, say, who took a short view of Othello

definitions.text: who took a short view of Othello

indicators.note: say means the word is spoken, so we want something that sounds like it

parts.note: a rhymer is one who writes verse

explanation.surface: A poet who dismissed Shakespeare's tragedy in brief.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Rymer's A Short View of Tragedy (1693) mocked Othello as 'a bloody farce'.
explanation.definitionFit: The critic Thomas Rymer attacked Othello in his book A Short View of Tragedy.

clue.text: A version of Roma, by way of La Romana's creator

indicators.note: a version of the word roma is a rearranged form of its letters

parts.note: via means by way of

explanation.surface: A take on Rome, through the writer of a novel about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of' rearranges ROMA into MORA; Alberto Moravia wrote La Romana (The Woman of Rome).
explanation.definitionFit: Alberto Moravia wrote the 1947 novel La Romana.

clue.text: He knew Cressida better than Troilus

definitions.text: He knew Cressida better than Troilus

parts.words: He knew Cressida better than Troilus
parts.note: in the Troy story Cressida is sent to the Greek camp and takes a Greek warrior as lover, deserting Troilus

explanation.surface: A rival who outdid the Trojan prince with his lover.
explanation.walkthrough: In Chaucer and Shakespeare, Cressida, once in the Greek camp, betrays Troilus for a Greek; 'knew' carries its biblical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek warrior Diomedes becomes Cressida's lover after she leaves Troy.

clue.text: "Tired of digging up potatoes, and spudding up " (Thomas Hardy)

definitions.text: "Tired of digging up potatoes, and spudding up " (Thomas Hardy)

parts.words: "Tired of digging up potatoes, and spudding up " (Thomas Hardy)
parts.note: the missing last word of the Hardy quotation names a coarse weed rooted out of fields

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hardy about farm labour, with its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is a broad-leaved weed (genus Rumex), dug out with a spud, a narrow spade.
explanation.definitionFit: These broad-leaved weeds are pulled out with a spud on farms.

clue.text: It has always supported art

parts.note: reads like a patron, but means the stand that holds a painter's canvas

explanation.surface: A loyal patron of the arts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supported art' suggests a benefactor; the support is literal, the frame a painter's canvas rests on.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter's stand holds the canvas up while the picture is made.

clue.text: Anita Brookner and Alan Sillitoe offered them in life

definitions.text: Anita Brookner and Alan Sillitoe offered them in life

parts.words: Anita Brookner and Alan Sillitoe offered them in life
parts.note: each novelist published a book called A Start in Life, so together they offered two

explanation.surface: Two novelists gave people a beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: Brookner's first novel (1981) and Sillitoe's 1970 novel share the title A Start in Life.
explanation.definitionFit: Both authors wrote a novel titled A Start in Life, so two beginnings.

clue.text: River goddess

definitions.meaning: the Thames at Oxford is known by this name
the Egyptian mother goddess, wife of Osiris

explanation.surface: A deity of the waters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Thames is called the Isis where it runs through Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford stretch of the Thames shares its name with the Egyptian goddess.

clue.text: Irritable habits of Meredith's girl?

parts.note: cross means irritable
ways are habits

explanation.surface: The bad-tempered manners of a novelist's heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's novel is Diana of the Crossways, so 'of Meredith's girl' completes her title.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's heroine is Diana of the Crossways, named for her house.

clue.text: Poetic PS

parts.note: a postscript to a poem: the short closing stanza of a ballade

explanation.surface: An afterthought in verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing short stanza of a ballade, addressed to the reader or patron, is a postscript to the poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The short final stanza of a ballade acts as a postscript.

clue.text: Seating arrangement in church is ideal, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words is ideal may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: The church's seats are well placed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IS IDEAL; sedilia are the stone seats for clergy set into the chancel's south wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedilia are the set of recessed stone seats for priests beside a church altar.

clue.text: "As a painter would a beggar under a triumphal arch" (W. S. Landor)

definitions.text: "As a painter would a beggar under a triumphal arch" (W. S. Landor)

parts.words: "As a painter would a beggar under a triumphal arch" (W. S. Landor)
parts.note: the quotation lacks a verb saying how a painter would place the beggar in the scene

explanation.surface: A Landor quotation about a painter's composition, with its verb missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing verb means to place or position, as a painter places a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: To place a figure in a setting, as a painter positions a beggar beneath an arch.
